briefOverview: Paul explains his God-given stewardship to reveal the mystery that Gentiles are fully included in Christ’s people, then prays that believers be strengthened to grasp Christ’s love and gives glory to God.
summary: Paul, writing as a prisoner for the sake of Gentiles, describes the divine revelation of the “mystery”: that Gentiles are fellow heirs, members of the same body, and sharers in God’s promise in Christ through the gospel. He emphasizes his calling to preach Christ’s unsearchable riches and to make known God’s once-hidden plan, so that even heavenly powers perceive God’s manifold wisdom through the church. Because of Christ, believers have confident access to God, so Paul urges them not to lose heart over his sufferings on their behalf. He prays that the Father would strengthen them inwardly by the Spirit, that Christ would dwell in their hearts by faith, and that being rooted in love they might comprehend the vastness of Christ’s love and be filled with all God’s fullness. He concludes with a doxology to the God who can do exceedingly more than believers ask or imagine, to whom belongs glory in the church and in Christ Jesus forever.
externalContext: Paul likely composed Ephesians during a period of imprisonment, often dated to his Roman custody in the early 60s CE. Ephesus was a major center in Roman Asia Minor, with a diverse population and significant religious activity, making issues of Jew–Gentile relations particularly salient. In Second Temple Jewish thought, a “mystery” (mysterion) often referred to a divine plan previously hidden but now disclosed by revelation. Early Christian communities recognized apostles and prophets as foundational witnesses who mediated this revelation by the Spirit. References to “principalities and powers” reflect a common ancient worldview in which spiritual beings or cosmic powers influence earthly affairs.
externalReferences: Paul’s commission to bring the gospel to the Gentiles is narrated in Acts 9:15 and affirmed in Galatians 2:7-9. The unveiling of the “mystery” long hidden but now revealed parallels Romans 16:25-26 and Colossians 1:26-27. The church’s witness before spiritual “principalities and powers” resonates with Ephesians 6:12 and the portrayal of Christ’s triumph over such powers in Colossians 2:15. Believers’ bold access to God through Christ is echoed in Hebrews 4:16 and 10:19-22.
practicalQuestions: Where might I be limiting who belongs in God’s people, and how can I embody the gospel’s full inclusion?
What would it look like to approach God with bold confidence in prayer this week?
How can I support and not lose heart when Christian leaders suffer for the gospel?
In what practices can I be rooted and grounded in love amid conflict or division?
How can my community display God’s manifold wisdom to a watching world?
uncertainAreas: The identity of the “principalities and powers” (v.10) is not fully specified and may include various spiritual or cosmic authorities; “the whole family in heaven and earth” (v.15) could refer to all God’s people and/or heavenly beings; the referent of the “breadth, length, depth, and height” (v.18) is unspecified (possibly Christ’s love or God’s redemptive plan); and “faith of him” (v.12) may mean faith in Christ or Christ’s faithfulness.
